title: Χῆνες καὶ γέρανοι
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 353. Text as printed. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Χῆνες καὶ γέρανοι τὸν αὐτὸν λειμῶνα ἐνέμοντο.
sentences.tr: Chēnes kai geranoi ton auton leimōna enemonto.
sentences.l: Geese and cranes were grazing the same meadow.
sentences.n: νέμομαι in the middle is 'to feed on, graze', and takes the accusative of the pasture itself; the active νέμω would be to put the flock out to graze. The imperfect sets the scene as something already going on when the story begins.

sentences.t: Ἐπιφανέντων δὲ αὐτοῖς θηρευτῶν, αἱ μὲν γέρανοι ἐλαφραὶ οὖσαι ἀπέπτησαν, οἱ δὲ χῆνες μείναντες διὰ τὸ βάρος τῶν σωμάτων συνελήφθησαν.
sentences.tr: Epiphanentōn de autois thēreutōn, hai men geranoi elaphrai ousai apeptēsan, hoi de chēnes meinantes dia to baros tōn sōmatōn synelēphthēsan.
sentences.l: And hunters having appeared to them, the cranes, being light, flew away, but the geese, having stayed behind because of the weight of their bodies, were taken.
sentences.i: But when hunters came in sight, the cranes were light and flew off, while the geese, held where they were by the weight of their bodies, were caught.
sentences.n: Ἐπιφανέντων … θηρευτῶν is a genitive absolute, a clause set outside the sentence's own grammar — one of the standing joints of the fable style. αἱ γέρανοι: γέρανος is feminine in gender, so the article is feminine whatever the birds' sex. μέν … δέ then sets the two flocks against each other, as it constantly does.

sentences.t: Οὕτω καὶ τῶν ἀνθρώπων, ἐπὰν πόλεμος ἐν πόλει γένηται, οἱ μὲν πένητες εὐπρόφοροι ὄντες, ῥᾳδίως ἀπὸ πόλεως εἰς ἑτέραν πόλιν διασῴζονται τῆς ἐλευθερίας μετέχοντες, οἱ δὲ πλούσιοι διὰ τὴν τῶν ὑπαρχόντων ὑπερβολὴν μένοντες πολλάκις δουλεύουσιν.
sentences.tr: Houtō kai tōn anthrōpōn, epan polemos en polei genētai, hoi men penētes euprophoroi ontes, rhāidiōs apo poleōs eis heteran polin diasōizontai tēs eleutherias metechontes, hoi de plousioi dia tēn tōn hyparchontōn hyperbolēn menontes pollakis douleuousin.
sentences.l: So too, among men, whenever war comes about in a city, the poor, being easily carried along, readily come safe through from one city to another, having a share in freedom, but the rich, staying behind because of the excess of their possessions, often serve as slaves.
sentences.i: So too, among men: when war breaks out in a city, the poor, with little to weigh them down, get safely away from one city to another and keep their freedom, while the rich, held fast by the sheer bulk of what they own, often live as slaves.
sentences.n: ἐπάν (ἐπεί + ἄν) with the subjunctive γένηται states the general case, 'whenever', not one occasion. τὰ ὑπάρχοντα, 'the things that are on hand', is the ordinary Greek for a man's property. μετέχω takes the genitive of what one has a share in. εὐπρόφορος is a rare compound; the sense wanted is plainly 'easily carried along, unencumbered', answering ἐλαφραί of the cranes above, but the word is uncommon enough that the rendering is a reading rather than a certainty.
